summary: Refex helps coal-fired power plants manage coal before it is burned and remove ash afterwards. It also has wind-turbine and smaller solar businesses.
description: A coal-fired power plant burns coal to make electricity. Coal must be unloaded, stored and moved to where it is needed; the ash left after burning must be collected and taken to a suitable reuse or disposal location. Refex takes on work along this chain under customer contracts.
money: Refex earns fees for the work covered by its contracts and can also earn from supplying materials such as coal or ash. It pays for workers, fuel, vehicles, machines, repairs and other business costs; the customer’s entire payment is not profit.
customers: Power plants that need coal and ash services, and businesses that buy materials such as coal or usable ash. In its other businesses, customers buy wind equipment, solar equipment or electricity. The contract determines who pays for each job or delivery.
drivers: How much work customers give it, the price agreed, transport distance, fuel and repair costs, and whether customers pay on time. Wind and solar activities have different costs from the coal and ash work.
products: Collecting fine ash and arranging a suitable destination
Removing ash previously stored in ash ponds
Loading and moving ash to its destination
Buying and supplying coal to customers
Unloading, storing and moving coal within a plant
Running and maintaining equipment that moves coal
Removing earth or rock above a deposit at a work site
Equipment that uses wind to generate electricity, through a subsidiary
productNote: Selected offerings within the issuer’s reported business boundary, including solar generation and solar-module trading in its audited annual segment disclosure. Refrigerants, power trading and green mobility are identified as discontinued in that disclosure; this does not establish completion of every legal transfer.

groups.title: Coal: getting fuel to where the plant needs it
groups.examples: Coal supply, unloading, storage and movement within the plant.
groups.explanation: Coal can arrive by truck or train. Depending on the contract, Refex may help unload it, keep it in the coal yard, move it, crush larger pieces and operate the equipment that feeds it towards use. A coal yard is the plant’s storage area for coal. The plant is buying a supply or service; Refex does not have to own the power plant to do this work.

groups.title: Ash: removing what is left after coal burns
groups.examples: Ash collection, loading, transport and arrangements for reuse or disposal.
groups.explanation: Burning coal leaves ash behind. Refex collects or removes the ash, loads it into vehicles and takes it to an agreed destination. Suitable ash may go to a cement maker or another approved use; other material needs an appropriate disposal route. The job includes arranging where the ash goes, not simply dropping it somewhere.

groups.title: Wind: a different business from moving coal and ash
groups.examples: Wind turbines through the Venwind Refex subsidiary.
groups.explanation: A wind turbine uses moving air to generate electricity. This business supplies equipment rather than carrying ash away from a power plant. It has to arrange production, delivery and the support promised to the customer. A subsidiary is a company controlled by another company.

groups.title: Solar: electricity and equipment
groups.examples: Solar-power generation and solar-panel trading reported in the company’s accounts.
groups.explanation: Solar generation means producing electricity using sunlight. Solar-panel trading means buying panels and selling them to customers. Those are different ways of earning money, even though both involve solar energy.

basics.title: What do “handling” and “transport” mean here?
basics.text: Handling means the practical work at the site: unloading, storing, loading, moving or preparing a material. Transport means carrying it from one place to another, such as taking ash from a power plant to a suitable destination. The exact tasks depend on the contract.

basics.title: What are fly ash and pond ash?
basics.text: Fly ash is fine ash collected from the gases produced when coal burns. Pond ash is ash that has been stored in an ash pond. Removing stored ash can require different machines and work from collecting fresh ash at a running plant.

basics.title: Who pays Refex, and for what?
basics.text: A power plant can pay Refex to carry out agreed coal or ash work. Refex can also receive money from customers buying materials it supplies. For example, a contract may cover removing and transporting ash, while a material sale involves a buyer paying for the material. The same payment arrangement should not be assumed for every job.

basics.title: A customer’s payment is different from profit
basics.text: Refex still has to pay drivers and other workers, buy fuel, use or hire equipment and pay for repairs. It also has costs of running and funding the business. What remains after the relevant costs and tax is profit. A completed job can be billed before the customer actually pays.

steps.title: The customer has a practical job to get done
steps.text: A power plant needs coal supplied or moved, or needs ash removed after burning coal. Refex and the customer agree which tasks Refex will carry out.

steps.title: Agree the work and payment
steps.text: The contract sets the work, responsibilities, price and payment terms. Check who pays for transport and where the material must be delivered.

steps.title: Send people, vehicles and machines to do the work
steps.text: Depending on the job, workers unload or move coal, collect ash, load vehicles and deliver materials. Refex pays the costs of doing the tasks it has agreed to take on.

steps.title: Confirm the work, send a bill and collect payment
steps.text: The customer checks the work or delivery under the contract. Refex bills for what it has earned and collects payment when due. It must fund fuel, wages and other bills while waiting for customer payments.

specifics.title: A longer truck journey can leave less profit
specifics.text: Moving material farther can use more fuel, driver time and vehicle capacity. Repairs, waiting at a site and an unsuitable destination can add costs too. More work is useful only if the agreed payment covers the costs of doing it.

specifics.title: A busy business can still be short of cash
specifics.text: Refex may have to pay wages and fuel bills before a customer pays its invoice. Money customers still owe is called receivables. If payment is delayed, Refex needs more money to keep the work going, even if it has recorded a profit.

specifics.title: Separate the present businesses from older ones
specifics.text: The audited annual accounts mark refrigerant gases, power trading and green mobility as discontinued operations: activities presented separately from the continuing business. That reporting label alone does not mean every legal transfer is complete. These older activities should not be mixed into today’s main service explanation.

specifics.title: A wind-equipment order still has to become a delivery
specifics.text: An announced order is a promise of future work. Equipment must still be made, delivered and accepted under the contract, and the customer must pay. Promised repairs or support after the sale can also cost money.

watch: Does the payment cover the cost of moving the material?
Distance, fuel and waiting time can change the cost of a job.

Read who pays for transport, where ash must go and what happens if fuel prices or delivery conditions change. A new contract announcement does not prove the work has started or that it will be profitable.
Are customers paying for completed work?
A bill sent to a customer is not yet money in the bank.
Look at money generated by day-to-day operations and the amount customers still owe. Check how long payments take and whether more money is tied up in unpaid bills as the business grows.
Does the business depend heavily on a few customers?
Work may fall if an important power plant slows down.

Look for the share of business coming from major customers and when contracts need renewal. Ask whether trucks, machines and workers could move to other jobs if a large contract ends or a plant stops operating.
Is the wind business delivering equipment and collecting payment?
Building equipment can require money before the customer pays.

Check which orders have become deliveries, whether production facilities are ready and what customers have paid in advance. Read who funds the subsidiary and who must pay if promised repairs or other commitments become due.
Which businesses are included in the accounts?
An old website page may still describe a business that has changed.

Use the latest signed accounts to separate continuing businesses from discontinued ones. Check which companies the group controls and any later transfer announcements; sharing the Refex name does not mean every business belongs to Refex Industries.
risks: Refex may still have to pay workers and fuel bills while waiting for customer payment.
A job costs more than expected
Longer routes, fuel prices, breakdowns or delays at a plant can reduce what remains from the agreed payment.
Ash does not reach a suitable destination
Collection, transport and reuse or disposal must meet the relevant rules. Refex needs appropriate destinations and permissions for the work it takes on.
New activities need money before they earn it
Wind equipment, new sites and other expansion can require spending before deliveries and customer payments arrive.
context: Use the latest accounts to check what has changed

Older Refex pages may describe businesses that the audited annual accounts now show separately as discontinued. Start with the signed accounts for the period, then check later announcements. Use the wider group’s website as a starting point, not as proof that every activity sits inside Refex Industries.
quiz: If Refex bills a customer for moving ash, is the whole bill its profit?
No. It still has to cover workers, fuel, vehicles, equipment, repairs and other costs. The bill may also be paid later, so recorded revenue, profit and cash received are different things.

financialNotes.title: Do not combine different operating scopes
financialNotes.text: The audited annual table identifies continuing and discontinued businesses separately. Use that annual reporting scope rather than combining an older group total with a newer business description. Segment results are not final group profit: read the unallocated-cost, financing, tax and discontinued-operation reconciliation.

financialNotes.title: Read operating cash and subsidiary obligations
financialNotes.text: Contract receivables, equipment investment, energy-business funding and guarantees can require cash despite accounting earnings. The segment table explains the source’s reported operating groups; it does not establish the cash return or profit of each customer contract.
